The biggest tradeoffs are climate, housing cost, and city scale. Phoenix is by far the largest city, while Raleigh has grown fastest since 2020. Denver and Austin have the highest incomes but also the most expensive housing; Raleigh offers a lower-cost middle ground, while Phoenix combines relatively moderate housing costs with the hottest climate.

Phoenix has a 2025 population of about 1.67 million, compared with 1.00 million in Austin, 741,000 in Denver, and 506,000 in Raleigh. Raleigh’s population grew 8.6% since 2020, faster than Austin’s 4.2%, Phoenix’s 3.3%, and Denver’s 3.2%. These figures describe the cities themselves, not their broader metro areas.

Housing is most expensive in Denver and Austin: median home values are $616,000 and $555,300, and median rents are $1,831 and $1,729. Raleigh and Phoenix are similar on rent—$1,572 and $1,582—but Raleigh’s median home value is slightly lower at $415,800 versus Phoenix’s $420,700. Homeownership is also more common in Phoenix and Raleigh than in Austin, where renters make up 56.6% of households.

Denver and Austin lead on median household income, at $94,718 and $93,658, followed by Raleigh at $85,395 and Phoenix at $81,332. Austin has the highest bachelor’s-degree attainment at 59.6%, compared with 56.5% in Denver, 54.0% in Raleigh, and 33.6% in Phoenix. Raleigh has the lowest unemployment rate in the comparison at 4.4%; the other cities range from 4.7% in Austin to 5.0% in Phoenix.

Climate is a clear differentiator. Phoenix is much hotter and drier: its normal July mean is 92.4°F with 0.81 inches of precipitation. Denver’s July mean is 74.8°F, but its normal January mean is only 32.1°F. Austin has the warmest winter of the four after Phoenix, with a January mean of 52.2°F, while Raleigh is cooler in winter and wetter through much of the year. These are NOAA 1991–2020 climate normals, not current-year conditions.

Commute times are fairly similar, from 23.0 minutes in Raleigh to 25.6 in Phoenix. Denver has the highest reported transit and walking shares—3.8% and 3.6%—while Austin has the highest work-from-home share at 30.7%. The data otherwise show driving as the dominant commute mode in all four cities.

Reported 2024 crime rates differ more noticeably. Denver has the highest violent- and property-crime rates in this dataset, at 993 and 4,761.6 per 100,000 residents. Phoenix reports the lowest property-crime rate, 2,325.3, while Austin and Raleigh are lower than Denver but higher than Phoenix on property crime. Austin and Raleigh have similar violent-crime rates—466.9 and 488.8—while Phoenix is higher at 799.6. These are city-level reported rates for 2024 and should not be treated as a complete measure of overall safety.

Overall, Austin combines high incomes, high educational attainment, strong work-from-home prevalence, and warm weather, but with comparatively costly housing. Denver offers high incomes and somewhat more non-driving commuting, balanced against the highest reported crime rates and colder winters. Raleigh stands out for rapid growth, lower housing costs, and the lowest unemployment rate. Phoenix offers the largest population, lower home costs than Austin or Denver, and relatively low reported property crime, but its extreme summer heat and lower educational-attainment figures are important tradeoffs.
